children: Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures hit a three-and-a-half-year high on Tuesday on reports that Moscow rejected a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea and struck port infrastructure in the region overnight, analysts said.
Futures reversed earlier weakness that followed a statement by Turkey that it was in contact with
and Ukraine about grain shipping via the Black Sea.
Russia attacked Ukraine's port infrastructure and a border crossing with Romania in the southern Black Sea region of Odessa overnight, Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the strike deliberately damaged a crossing point on the border with Romania as well as export infrastructure.

The escalating tensions have cast uncertainty over global grain supplies. Attacks in recent months have halted almost all grain shipments through Black Sea ports and the Sea of Azov, which used to account for 70% of all Russian grain exports. Traders remain on edge about the risks of prolonged interruption to both Russian and Ukrainian grain exports from the region.

Prices had fallen after Turkey said on Monday that it had prepared a plan for the safe passage of grain via the Black Sea. But Russia rejected a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, saying it would not bring the prospect of a peaceful resolution to
any closer, Interfax reported on Tuesday, citing Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko.
CBOT December soft red winter wheat (WZ26) futures settled 8-1/2 cents higher to $7.82-1/2 per bushel.
K.C. December hard red winter wheat (KWZ26) rose 7-1/4 cents to $8.45-1/4 per bushel.
Minneapolis December wheat (MWEZ26) settled 13-3/4 cents higher to $7.76-3/4 per bushel.
